qc.notes: Every episode is ONE unbroken 8-second shot of a real, recognisable place struck by a REAL kind of natural disaster at an impossible scale. Fail the shot if the camera pans, tracks, orbits or follows the event instead of staying locked, if any cut, fade, dissolve or scene reset appears inside the shot, or if the disaster is not already at full strength in the very first frame. The disaster must be a real type (tsunami, whirlpool, hurricane, tornado, earthquake, fissure, landslide, eruption, pyroclastic flow, glacier collapse, dust storm, lightning storm): an invented event or a science-fiction element is a failure. A human-made structure of known size must stay in frame so the scale reads. Readable text, captions, subtitles, logos, watermarks and closing cards are automatic failures. Human figures, bodies, panicking crowds and close-ups of inhabited buildings being destroyed are forbidden: this channel shows physics and scale, not casualties. The geography must stay a believable version of the real place named in the plan; invented place names are a failure. Record any of these under issues. A map-like graphic, drawn borders, outlines, grid lines or labels anywhere in the frame are a failure.

art_style: Natural documentary photograph in motion, composed for vertical 9:16: true-colour footage of the real Earth from a high-altitude camera, with the look of astronaut photography from the International Space Station. Real cloud cover casting cloud shadows on the ground, sun glint on water, soft atmospheric haze and a thin blue limb along the top edge. The named place keeps its real coastline, rivers, relief, ice and city-light pattern exactly as it looks from above, as clean, unmarked natural terrain. The disaster is made of real matter, water, cloud, ash, ice, dust or fire, with true weight, motion and light at a scale the real Earth could never produce. Low-to-moderate tonal contrast, restrained true-to-life saturation, neutral white balance, open shadow detail, protected highlights, fine sensor grain, stable exposure. A human-made structure of known size stays visible so the scale reads at once. Static camera: one fixed position, orientation, focal length and exposure for the whole shot. Pure photography: the image carries zero map lines, borders, labels, text or graphics.
